Question 1: Signal strength and correlated substitutes

Answer

Note

A note on random-number generation. The simulation below draws with rng = np.random.default_rng(43246) (NumPy’s modern Generator API) rather than the legacy np.random.seed() + np.random.randn() pattern. This matters here specifically because sklearn.linear_model.Lasso/ElasticNet call check_random_state(None) internally on every .fit() call — even under the default selection="cyclic" — which silently advances the legacy global RNG’s internal position. With the legacy pattern, that means the exact sequence of simulated datasets would depend on how many models get fit per repetition, so Question 1 (one lasso fit per repetition/penalty) and Question 2 (lasso and elastic net) would silently end up simulating different data even with the same seed — breaking the requirement that both questions “produce the same datasets.” A default_rng() generator is a separate, local object that .fit() never touches, so this can’t happen.

Part a

All 800 fits converged: True

As λ\lambda increases from 0.080.08 to 0.240.24, mean |β̂j||\hat\beta_j| falls monotonically for every covariate (Table , figures above) — the usual ℓ1\ell_1 shrinkage/soft-thresholding effect. Selection frequency (Table , figures above) falls for every covariate as λ\lambda grows, but at very different rates. X3X_3 (true coefficient 0.300.30) is selected in essentially every replicate at the smallest penalty (0.9800.980) and remains the most frequently selected covariate throughout, still at 0.7150.715 at λ=0.24\lambda = 0.24. X1X_1, X2X_2, and X4X_4 (true coefficient 0.150.15 each) start noticeably lower (0.530.53–0.830.83) and fall faster, with X4X_4 collapsing to 0.1500.150 by λ=0.24\lambda=0.24. The pure noise covariates X5,…,X10X_5,\dots,X_{10} (true coefficient 00) start around 0.310.31–0.420.42 at λ=0.08\lambda = 0.08 — nontrivial, since with n=120n=120 and ten correlated-with-noise draws some spurious selection is expected at a small penalty — but are driven toward zero rapidly, averaging about 0.050.05 by λ=0.18\lambda = 0.18 and under 0.010.01 by λ=0.24\lambda = 0.24. This ordering matches the size of the true coefficient: a larger true signal survives a larger penalty before its estimated effect is shrunk below the point where it gets thresholded to exactly zero.

Part b

lambda=0.08: only_X1=0.465 only_X2=0.465 both=0.060 neither=0.010
lambda=0.12: only_X1=0.475 only_X2=0.440 both=0.035 neither=0.050
lambda=0.18: only_X1=0.445 only_X2=0.405 both=0.030 neither=0.120
lambda=0.24: only_X1=0.350 only_X2=0.310 both=0.030 neither=0.310

The marginal selection frequencies of X1X_1 and X2X_2 are close at every λ\lambda (Table ) — 0.5250.525 vs. 0.5250.525 at λ=0.08\lambda=0.08, narrowing to 0.3800.380 vs. 0.3400.340 at λ=0.24\lambda=0.24 — consistent with corr(X1,X2)=0.999\operatorname{corr}(X_1,X_2) = 0.999 and identical true coefficients (0.150.15 each): the two variables carry essentially the same information about YY, so there is no structural reason for lasso to favor one over the other on average, and the small gap reflects only sampling variation from the specific noise draw ZZ used to construct X2X_2 from X1X_1 in each replicate.

As λ\lambda increases, both selected declines from 0.0600.060 to 0.0300.030 while neither selected rises sharply, from 0.0100.010 at λ=0.08\lambda=0.08 to 0.3100.310 at λ=0.24\lambda=0.24; only X1X_1 and only X2X_2 remain the dominant outcomes at the smaller penalties, together accounting for over 90%90\% of replicates at λ=0.08\lambda=0.08, though that combined share falls to about 66%66\% by λ=0.24\lambda=0.24 as neither grows. This is the signature lasso behavior under near-collinearity: because X1X_1 and X2X_2 are almost interchangeable predictors, the ℓ1\ell_1 penalty makes it cheaper to load the shared effect onto a single member of the pair and zero out the other than to keep two nearly redundant coefficients active simultaneously. Which one “wins” is sensitive to the noise realization in a given replicate, producing a sparse fitted rule that omits one member of the pair even though both appear with equal weight (0.150.15 each) in the true generating equation. As λ\lambda grows further, it becomes cheap enough to drop even the single retained variable, so neither grows to over 30%30\% of replicates by λ=0.24\lambda=0.24 while both falls to half its λ=0.08\lambda=0.08 level.

Part c

At every λ\lambda, freq(X3)>freq(X4)≫avg. freq(X5,…,X10)\text{freq}(X_3) > \text{freq}(X_4) \gg \text{avg. freq}(X_5,\dots,X_{10}) (Table ): at λ=0.08\lambda=0.08 this is 0.9800.980 vs. 0.8300.830 vs. 0.3620.362, and by λ=0.24\lambda=0.24 the gap has widened in relative terms to 0.7150.715 vs. 0.1500.150 vs. 0.0090.009. This tracks the ordering of true coefficient magnitude (β3=0.30>β4=0.15>β5=…=β10=0\beta_3=0.30 > \beta_4=0.15 > \beta_5=\dots=\beta_{10}=0): a larger true coefficient produces a larger, more reliably detectable in-sample correlation with YY, so a larger λ\lambda is required to push its estimate below the soft-threshold. The noise block’s average frequency is not negligible at the smallest penalty (0.3620.362) — with ten covariates and n=120n=120, a few spurious correlations are expected to survive a weak penalty — but it decays roughly forty-fold from λ=0.08\lambda=0.08 to λ=0.24\lambda=0.24, confirming that penalty strength is doing most of the work of separating signal from noise once λ\lambda is large enough.

The (X1,X2)(X_1,X_2) results show why a fitted zero does not establish that the population coefficient is zero, and a nonzero fit does not establish unique importance. In a replicate where lasso selects only X2X_2, the true β1=0.15\beta_1 = 0.15 is identical to β2\beta_2 — X1X_1 is just as related to YY marginally, but was dropped only because X2X_2 already absorbs nearly the same information. Symmetrically, the nonzero β̂2\hat\beta_2 in that replicate is not evidence that X2X_2 uniquely drives YY: it stands in for a shared effect that could equally have been attributed to X1X_1 in a different sample, as the near-equal magnitudes of only X1X_1 (0.4650.465 at λ=0.08\lambda=0.08) and only X2X_2 (0.4650.465) in Table confirm. Under high correlation, lasso’s selection pattern reflects which member of a redundant group happened to be picked in that sample — not which variable is structurally “the” important one.

Question 2: Elastic net with an equal penalty mix

Answer

Lasso: all 800 fits converged: True. Elastic net: all 800 fits converged: True.

Part a

The elastic-net selection frequencies (Table , Figure ) are higher than lasso’s for every covariate at every λ\lambda (Table is entirely positive). The largest gains, by far, belong to X1X_1 and X2X_2: their selection frequencies jump from roughly 0.340.34–0.530.53 under lasso (Question 1) to 0.930.93–0.990.99 under elastic net, a gain that grows with λ\lambda (from about +0.44+0.44 at λ=0.08\lambda=0.08 to about +0.56+0.56–0.600.60 at λ=0.24\lambda=0.24). X4X_4 also gains substantially, and its gain keeps growing across the whole grid — from +0.105+0.105 at λ=0.08\lambda=0.08 up to +0.510+0.510 at λ=0.24\lambda=0.24, the largest single gain in the table. X3X_3, already near-saturated under lasso, gains only modestly until the largest penalty (+0.020+0.020 at λ=0.08\lambda=0.08 rising to +0.235+0.235 at λ=0.24\lambda=0.24). The noise covariates X5,…,X10X_5,\dots,X_{10} gain more moderately in absolute terms (+0.12+0.12 to +0.35+0.35) but represent the biggest relative increase, since their lasso baseline was already small. In short: the covariates that change the most, and in the clearest direction (upward), are the near-collinear pair X1,X2X_1, X_2 — precisely the pair the ℓ2\ell_2 component was designed to keep together.

Part b

Under elastic net, the “both selected” outcome dominates completely: it is 0.9450.945 at λ=0.08\lambda = 0.08 and stays at 0.9250.925–0.9700.970 across the whole grid, compared to only 0.0300.030–0.0600.060 under lasso (Table from Question 1). “Only X1X_1” and “only X2X_2” — the outcomes that dominated under lasso — are now rare (each at or under 0.0250.025 at every λ\lambda), and “neither” stays negligible except at the largest penalty (0.0500.050 at λ=0.24\lambda=0.24, versus 0.0050.005–0.0150.015 elsewhere). So yes: the two covariates are now properly selected together almost every time, essentially resolving the “arbitrary single-variable pick” behavior seen under lasso.

This is exactly the elastic net’s designed grouping effect. Lasso’s penalty is λ∥β∥1=λ∑j|βj|\lambda \|\beta\|_1 = \lambda \sum_j |\beta_j|, which is invariant to how a fixed total coefficient budget is split across two identical, highly correlated columns — putting all the weight on one variable costs exactly the same, in ℓ1\ell_1 norm, as putting all the weight on the other, or anything in between, so the optimizer has no reason to prefer splitting the coefficient. Adding a squared ℓ2\ell_2 term, 1−α2λ∥β∥22=1−α2λ∑jβj2\tfrac{1-\alpha}{2}\lambda \|\beta\|_2^2 = \tfrac{1-\alpha}{2}\lambda \sum_j \beta_j^2, breaks that degeneracy: because the square is a strictly convex function, splitting a fixed total coefficient cc evenly between two identical, perfectly (or near-perfectly) correlated predictors, β1=β2=c/2\beta_1=\beta_2=c/2, gives a strictly smaller ℓ2\ell_2 penalty (2⋅(c/2)2=c2/22\cdot(c/2)^2 = c^2/2) than concentrating it on one, β1=c,β2=0\beta_1=c,\ \beta_2=0 (penalty c2c^2). The elastic net therefore actively prefers to spread the coefficient across both near-duplicate covariates rather than arbitrarily picking one, which is why (X1,X2)(X_1, X_2) are selected as a pair almost every time rather than individually.

Part c

The noise covariates are still screened out as λ\lambda increases under elastic net — their average frequency falls monotonically from 0.6560.656 at λ=0.08\lambda=0.08 to 0.1820.182 at λ=0.24\lambda=0.24 — but at every λ\lambda this is substantially higher than the lasso baseline (0.362→0.0090.362 \to 0.009 over the same grid), roughly 1.8×1.8\times to 20×20\times as large. This is a direct consequence of the mixing: at a given numerical λ\lambda, sklearn’s ElasticNet objective applies only αλ=0.5λ\alpha\lambda = 0.5\lambda of ℓ1\ell_1 weight (the rest of the penalty budget goes to the ℓ2\ell_2 term), so the effective ℓ1\ell_1 threshold that drives small coefficients exactly to zero is roughly half as strong as lasso’s at the same λ\lambda. A weaker ℓ1\ell_1 threshold means noise coefficients that would have been soft-thresholded to zero under lasso survive under elastic net, which is why the noise block is screened out far more slowly.

Combining parts (b) and (c): the elastic net achieves near-complete joint selection of (X1,X2)(X_1, X_2) — “both” ≥0.925\geq 0.925 — across the entire grid λ∈{0.08,0.12,0.18,0.24}\lambda \in \{0.08, 0.12, 0.18, 0.24\}, but noise-block selection frequency only drops to a comparably low range (0.1820.182, still well above lasso’s 0.0090.009 at the same λ\lambda) at the largest penalty, λ=0.24\lambda = 0.24. So λ=0.24\lambda = 0.24 is the penalty in this grid that comes closest to simultaneously keeping the correlated pair together (both selected 92.5%92.5\% of the time) while most effectively screening out the noise covariates (down to 18.2%18.2\% average selection, versus 3131–66%66\% at the smaller penalties) — though even at λ=0.24\lambda=0.24 noise selection remains well above the lasso benchmark, reflecting the inherent trade-off of the weaker ℓ1\ell_1 threshold built into the equal-mix elastic net.

Question 3: Coordinate descent and the lasso path

Answer

Show the workflow 
def soft(a, lam):
    return np.sign(a) * max(abs(a) - lam, 0.0)

def coord_descent(Xs, Yc, lam, beta_init, tol=1e-8, max_iter=100000):
    beta = beta_init.copy()
    n_, p_ = Xs.shape
    for it in range(1, max_iter + 1):
        max_change = 0.0
        for j in range(p_):
            # residual leaving covariate j out of the current fit
            resid_j = Yc - Xs @ beta + Xs[:, j] * beta[j]
            a_j = np.mean(Xs[:, j] * resid_j)
            new_beta_j = soft(a_j, lam)
            max_change = max(max_change, abs(new_beta_j - beta[j]))
            beta[j] = new_beta_j
        if max_change < tol:
            return beta, it, True
    return beta, max_iter, False

beta_path = np.zeros((len(lambdas), p))
converged_flags = []
iters_used = []

beta_curr = np.zeros(p)   # warm start: begin the grid at beta = 0
for i, lam in enumerate(lambdas):
    beta_curr, iters, conv = coord_descent(Xs, Yc, lam, beta_curr)  # warm start from previous lambda
    beta_path[i, :] = beta_curr
    converged_flags.append(conv)
    iters_used.append(iters)

all_converged = all(converged_flags)
lambda_max = np.max(np.abs(Xs.T @ Yc / n))
beta_ols = np.linalg.lstsq(Xs, Yc, rcond=None)[0]

Part a

All 10 fits converged (max. coefficient change <10−8< 10^{-8}): True. Iterations per grid value: [1, 2, 2, 2, 6, 6, 6, 6, 6, 6]. λmax=∥1nX⊤ỹ∥∞=2.1270\lambda_{\max} = \|\, \tfrac{1}{n}X^\top \tilde y\,\|_\infty = 2.1270.

Grid values at or above λmax\lambda_{\max}: [2.5]. All slopes zero there: True.

All ten fits converged, and convergence was fast throughout — never more than 6 full cycles, and in some cases just 1–2, because each fit was warm-started from the coefficients found at the adjacent (larger) λ\lambda. Consistent with the theory, λmax≈2.127\lambda_{\max} \approx 2.127, and at the one grid value at or above it, λ=2.5\lambda = 2.5, all slopes are exactly zero. At the very next grid value, λ=2.0<λmax\lambda = 2.0 < \lambda_{\max}, β̂2\hat\beta_2 has already become nonzero (−0.127-0.127) — exactly what λmax\lambda_{\max} is supposed to mark: the largest penalty at which any coefficient first enters the model.

Part b

As λ\lambda decreases from 2.52.5 toward 0.030.03 (equivalently, moving toward more negative logλ\log\lambda, since log(2.5)≈0.92\log(2.5)\approx 0.92 and log(0.03)≈−3.51\log(0.03)\approx -3.51), the covariates enter the model in this order: X2X_2 first (nonzero already at λ=2.0\lambda = 2.0), then X1X_1 (nonzero starting at λ=0.6\lambda = 0.6), while X3X_3 never enters at any grid value. This order matches the sizes of the true coefficients: |β2|=2.0>|β1|=1.0>|β3|=0|\beta_2| = 2.0 > |\beta_1| = 1.0 > |\beta_3| = 0. Because the covariates are independent standard normals here (no near-collinearity as in Q1–Q2), the score aj=1nxj⊤ỹa_j = \frac{1}{n}x_j^\top \tilde y that drives the soft-threshold update is, in expectation, proportional to the true coefficient βj\beta_j; the covariate with the largest true effect produces the largest score and so is the first to exceed the shrinking penalty λ\lambda and enter the model, with smaller true effects entering only once λ\lambda has fallen further, and a zero true effect never entering (at least not from real signal — see part c).

Part c

X3X_3 has a true population coefficient of zero, and in this run it stays exactly zero at every grid value, including the smallest penalty λ=0.03\lambda = 0.03 — it never enters the path. This happens because X3X_3’s score a3=1nx3⊤ỹa_3 = \frac{1}{n}x_3^\top \tilde y never exceeds 0.030.03 in absolute value for this particular sample, so the soft-threshold S(a3,0.03)=sign(a3)(|a3|−0.03)+S(a_3, 0.03) = \mathrm{sign}(a_3)(|a_3| - 0.03)_+ is zero at every λ\lambda tried.

Comparing the lasso fit at λ=0.03\lambda = 0.03 with ordinary least squares on the same standardized design: β̂1=0.970\hat\beta_1 = 0.970 (lasso) vs. 1.0081.008 (OLS), β̂2=−2.213\hat\beta_2 = -2.213 (lasso) vs. −2.244-2.244 (OLS), and β̂3=0\hat\beta_3 = 0 (lasso) vs. 0.0280.028 (OLS, nonzero because OLS applies no penalty at all). The two fits are close but not identical for two related reasons. First, λ=0.03\lambda = 0.03 is small but strictly positive, so lasso still applies a small amount of soft-thresholding shrinkage to every coordinate — pulling β̂1\hat\beta_1 and β̂2\hat\beta_2 slightly toward zero relative to their unpenalized OLS values — which is why lasso’s magnitudes are both slightly smaller than OLS’s in absolute value. Second, and more visibly for X3X_3, lasso’s soft-threshold sets any coefficient whose score falls below λ\lambda in absolute value to exactly zero, while OLS has no such mechanism and instead returns whatever small nonzero value (0.0280.028) best fits the sampling noise in that column. As λ→0\lambda \to 0 the coordinate descent solution converges to the OLS solution exactly (since the penalty vanishes), so the residual gap seen here at λ=0.03\lambda = 0.03 reflects the last bit of shrinkage and thresholding still present at that grid’s smallest value.

Question 4: Tuning and comparing penalized regressions for diabetes prediction

Answer

Setup notes

Because diabetes.csv carries no explicit row identifier, the join to diabetes-split-folds.csv is done by row position: a sequential row_id (1,…,4421,\dots,442) is attached to diabetes.csv in file order and matched against the row_id column already present in the split file. This assumption is checked directly: row_id in the split file is exactly the sequence 1,…,4421,\dots,442, every training row carries a fold label 1,…,101,\dots,10, and every test row’s fold label is missing — both assertions above pass, supporting the row-order join.

Cross-validation results

The three tuned fits are nearly indistinguishable: minimum cross-validation MSEs of about 3071.23071.2 (lasso), 3073.53073.5 (ridge), and 3073.43073.4 (elastic net), each with fold-based standard errors around 240240. The gap between the three methods is small compared with the displayed fold-to-fold variability — this descriptive comparison nominates a winner for this particular fold assignment, but it does not establish that any one method is truly superior for this prediction problem.

Selected model and final test evaluation

Selected covariates: age, sex, bmi, bp, s1, s2, s4, s5, s6.

Dropped: s3.

Lasso is the nominal winner, at a penalty of α≈0.10\alpha \approx 0.10. The selected fit keeps nine of the ten covariates (all but s3), with training MSE about 2908.42908.4 and a final test MSE of about 2732.42732.4 — evaluated exactly once, after the model and its penalty were already fixed by the cross-validation comparison, so this is an honest assessment of the complete selected procedure. The test error happens to fall slightly below the validation error here, but this ordering is itself a feature of this particular test split and could reverse under a different one. Because the comparison across lasso, ridge, and elastic net used the same ten folds throughout and the test rows were untouched until the method and penalty were both fixed, a different fold assignment could plausibly have nominated ridge or elastic net instead without changing anything about the validity of the procedure — the cross-validation table and plots, not the identity of the winner, are what justify the selection.
